meta.title: Take business rules out of your code
meta.description: Ordo is an open-source business rule engine. Pricing, risk and approval logic lives in rule files with tests and versions. See what a change affects before you ship it, and ship it without a redeploy.

hero.subtitle: Pricing, risk and approval logic changes all the time. Write it as rule files with tests and versions, see which decisions a change moves before you ship it, and ship it without a redeploy. People can write the rules, and so can AI.

problem.title: Rules buried in code turn into a mess

items.title: Hard to find
items.desc: Discounts, limits and risk thresholds are spread across if/else branches in dozens of files. Nobody can say for sure what the policy is today.

items.title: Hard to change
items.desc: Moving one number means a full release. Product and risk teams wait in the engineering queue.

items.title: Hard to explain
items.desc: When something goes wrong, it is hard to say why an order was declined, or what the rule looked like last month.

problem.ai_note: AI now writes code fast, and these branches grow faster with it. The generated code runs, but nobody can promise it matches the policy.

workflow.title: Write it down, test it, see it, ship it

steps.title: Write rule files
steps.desc: Branches, decision tables and expressions live in JSON or YAML, in git next to your code. Inputs are declared with types, and money is exact decimal.

steps.title: Run the tests
steps.desc: Every ruleset carries its own test cases. ordo test runs them locally and in CI, with no server to start.

steps.title: See every step
steps.desc: ordo trace prints each step a run took and every value along the way. When someone asks why a payment was blocked, you have the answer.

steps.title: Ship it
steps.desc: Embed the same rules in a Rust program, call them over HTTP or gRPC, or run them in the browser as WASM. A run takes microseconds.

impact.title: Green tests do not mean nothing broke
impact.p1: The risk team wants to block payments from a score of 65 instead of 70. After the edit, all 9 tests still pass.
impact.p2: ordo impact runs the edit next to the last commit: the 9 test cases plus 121 probe inputs generated on both sides of every threshold. Five of those inputs move from "challenge" to "block", such as a long-standing customer paying 5000 from abroad on a new phone.
impact.p3: Whether a person or an AI made the edit, the effect is right there. Coding agents call the same check through ordo mcp and look before they commit.
points: Compares against the last version in git

packs.title: Start from a rule pack
packs.desc: Common business decisions, already written and tested. Copy one and change the numbers to your own policy.

items.name: Credit approval
items.desc: A personal loan application: approve, send to manual review, or decline.

items.name: Promo stacking
items.desc: Which promotions apply at checkout, how far they stack, and what the customer pays.

items.name: Fraud scoring
items.desc: A card payment: allow, add a challenge, or block.

packs.note: A rule pack is a plain Ordo project. Rules your team writes can be shared the same way.

studio.title: Rules your non-engineers can read and review
studio.desc: Studio draws the same rules as a flow and as a decision table. Business teams read the logic, run tests and request releases there. Engineers keep working with files and git.
bullets: One ruleset, shown as a flow or as a decision table
Run tests in Studio and see expected against actual
Field catalog, decision contracts, version history and release approvals

guard.title: The same engine keeps coding agents in bounds
guard.desc: Before an agent runs a command, it goes through your local rules: allow, deny, or ask you first. The policy is an Ordo project with tests and a log. Works with Claude Code, Codex CLI and Cursor.
guard.cmd_caption: One command writes a policy and wires up the hook

ecosystem.title: One engine, and everything around it
ecosystem.desc: The engine gets the rules right, and fast. The CLI, Studio, SDKs and rule packs are built on top of it, and you can build your own tools there too.

stats.label: per rule run on the bytecode VM

items.name: Engine
items.desc: A rule engine in Rust: bytecode VM plus Cranelift JIT. Embed it, or call it over HTTP, gRPC or WASM.

items.name: CLI and MCP
items.desc: init, test, trace, impact. Coding agents call the same commands over MCP.

items.name: Studio
items.desc: Visual editing, tests, version history and release approvals.

items.name: SDKs
items.desc: Go, Python and Java clients, plus Vue and React editor components.

items.name: Rule packs
items.desc: Business rule projects you can run as is, tests included.

cta.title: Run a rule pack
cta.desc: Install the CLI, step into a rule pack, change a threshold, and see what impact tells you.

footer.desc: An open-source business rule engine. Keep the decisions that change often in rules with tests and versions, so people and AI can change them safely.
